title: She Said, “You Are Imprisoned.” I Said, “It Does No Harm”
intro: Ibn al-Mu'tazz records that Ali ibn al-Jahm addressed these verses to the caliph al-Mutawakkil from prison. A woman sees disgrace in his confinement, and he answers with a sword in its sheath and fire held inside a stone. Only then does he ask Ahmad ibn Abi Du'ad to carry his complaint to court. His accusers have been heard in his absence, and the prisoner wants the chance to answer them.

translation: She said, “You are in prison.” I said, “It does me
no harm. What Indian blade is never sheathed?”
1.sharh: Her news already sounds like a judgement. His answer makes the sheath a measure of the weapon’s worth even while it keeps the blade out of sight.

translation: Have you never seen the lion keep to his thicket
in pride, while the rabble of beasts comes and goes?
2.sharh: The lion can afford to stay in his den. It is the lesser beasts that have to make a show of coming and going.

translation: If the sun were never hidden
from your eyes, the pole star’s companion could never shine.
3.sharh: The little northern star becomes visible when the sun is out of sight. Its moment of prominence tells us how much greater the absent light is.

translation: The full moon too is overtaken by the dark of the month.
Those days pass, and it looks born again.
4.sharh: The moon’s disappearance belongs to a cycle. Here the resemblance to prison lies in the possibility of returning with the freshness of something newly made.

translation: The cloud holds the rain confined. You never see it
but its first drops come with wind and thunder.
5.sharh: A cloud keeps its store of water out of sight. The noise and movement at the first rain make the release all the more conspicuous.

translation: Fire lies hidden in its stones.
No one can warm himself unless the firesticks rouse it.
6.sharh: A spark has to be struck before anyone can sit by the fire. The stone looks cold throughout the time the poet imagines fire living within it.

translation: The joints of the long spears are straightened
only by the straightening clamp and a glowing brand.
7.sharh: The maker heats the shaft and works it in a clamp. Confinement has acquired a new possibility in this image, that pressure can improve what it encloses.

translation: The turns of time come first and come again.
Wealth is a loan, acquired and spent.
8.sharh: Reversals are recurrent visitors. Even the wealth a person calls his own behaves like a loan, so his present circumstances need not be permanent either.

translation: Every state of affairs has its successor.
Often the thing you hate clears to reveal what you welcome.
9.sharh: A hated event can act like a covering. What emerges when it clears may give someone reason to welcome the outcome of the very thing he feared.

translation: Let no blow dealt you by ill-starred time
make you despair of release from distress.
10.sharh: Time is made into an assailant that throws misfortune at its victim. The force of the blow tells him little about his chances of relief.

translation: How often death has stepped over a sick man
who lived, while his doctor and visitors died.
11.sharh: Everyone in the sickroom seems to know who is most in danger. Death steps past the bed and takes the healthy people gathered around it.

translation: Patience. Patience brings ease in its wake,
and no hand can reach as high as the caliph’s.
12.sharh: For the first time release has a possible human agent. After so many changes in nature and fortune comes the hand that can order the prison opened.

translation: Prison, unless some foul and shameful act brought you there,
is a fine lodging to come to.
13.sharh: His praise of prison has a condition. What led a person there can be disgraceful, but the fact that he is there proves nothing about his honour.

translation: A house that renews a noble man’s distinction.
He receives visits, pays none and has people serve him.
14.sharh: Being unable to go out can be made to look like rank. In this portrait everyone comes to the prisoner’s door, like petitioners attending a lord.

translation: If prison had this single merit only,
no slave at court can shame you by barring the door.
15.sharh: A petitioner at court must submit to someone who controls access. The prisoner gives his exclusion a bitter advantage, freedom from waiting on the doorkeepers.

translation: Ahmad ibn Abi Du'ad, every grave affair
brings a call for you, Ahmad.
16.sharh: He calls on the chief judge by name twice. The praise also lays a claim on his attention, since this is exactly the kind of grave business for which others seek him.

translation: Carry word to the Commander of the Faithful.
Between me and him lie enemies’ meddling and unending fears.
17.sharh: He needs a messenger because his opponents have already reached the ruler with their talk. An appeal sent through the judge might catch up with their accusations.

translation: You, kinsmen of the Prophet Muhammad,
have first claim to uphold what Muhammad laid down.
18.sharh: The Abbasids claimed descent from the Prophet’s uncle. Invoking that kinship lets the prisoner ask the dynasty to practise the justice it inherits.

translation: Whatever goodness there is, you are its people.
Good was the soil you sprang from, good your stock.
19.sharh: He pictures the ruling family as plants well rooted in good soil. The compliment prepares a test of whether its present conduct lives up to that origin.

translation: Is it fair, cousin of Muhammad,
to draw one adversary close and keep the other away?
20.sharh: He identifies the procedural wrong with two movements of the ruler’s hand, bringing one litigant near and sending the other away.

translation: Those who carried falsehood to you
are enemies of your favour, which no one can deny.
21.sharh: He presents the informers as enemies of the ruler’s own bounty. In his account, their false reports have made favour give way to punishment.

translation: They attended while we were away and ruled on us.
A man who is present has an advantage over the absent.
22.sharh: The accusers have effectively judged the case they were meant to present. One party’s absence explains how a verdict could look convincing.

translation: If one hearing before you brought both parties together,
the straightest course would become clear to you.
23.sharh: A single shared hearing would do more than all the one-sided reports. The straight road is the judgement the ruler could reach after hearing both.

translation: If I outlast these times and one day gain
a seat in the presence of the sovereign caliph,
24.sharh: The imagined hearing begins with the smallest concession, a place to sit. The unfinished sentence keeps the prisoner waiting until the next bayt.

translation: and my opponent argues and I argue my own case,
my proofs will prevail. The other man will fail.
25.sharh: The repeated Arabic root for arguing gives each side a turn to speak. Only after that exchange does he claim victory.

translation: God brings his decree to pass among his creatures.
To him tomorrow is our departure and our coming to water.
26.sharh: The verbs behind the paired nouns describe going to water and leaving it. However their paths run, prisoner, accuser and sovereign all ultimately answer to God.

translation: If I die, the man who plotted against me will hardly last.
The appointed meeting will bring us both together.
27.sharh: Death might defeat his request for a hearing at court. It cannot keep the accuser from eventually meeting him on equal terms.

translation: For what offence has our honour become spoil
that a vile man can loudly advertise?
28.sharh: At the close, reputation has become loot open to the first plunderer. The prisoner still wants to know what charge justified handing it over.

1.1.5.head: ضائِر
1.1.5.meaning: Causing harm. The reciter sounds closer to “apparent”. The diwan reads “harmful”, with “harmful to me” also transmitted.

1.2.3.head: مُهَنَّد
1.2.3.meaning: A sword of Indian steel, proverbial for its quality.

2.1.5.head: غيل
2.1.5.meaning: The thicket that shelters a lion.

3.2.5.head: الفَرقَد
3.2.5.meaning: Al-Farqad, one of two stars near the north celestial pole.

4.1.3.head: السِّرار
4.1.3.meaning: The dark nights at the end of a lunar month.

6.2.2.head: اِصطَلى
6.2.2.meaning: To warm oneself at a fire.

7.1.1.head: الزّاعِبِيَّة
7.1.1.meaning: Za'biyya, a celebrated kind of spear.

7.2.2.head: الثِّقاف
7.2.2.meaning: A clamp used to straighten a spear shaft.

11.2.4.head: العُوَّد
11.2.4.meaning: The people who visit a sick person.

13.1.4.head: غَشِيَ
13.1.4.meaning: To go to a place or enter it.

13.2.4.head: المُتَوَرَّد
13.2.4.meaning: A place to which someone comes to lodge.

15.2.3.head: الحِجاب
15.2.3.meaning: The court practice of controlling access to the ruler.

15.2.4.head: الأَعبُد
15.2.4.meaning: Enslaved attendants, here the palace doorkeepers.

16.1.2-5.head: أَحمَد بن أَبي دُؤاد
16.1.2-5.meaning: Ahmad ibn Abi Du'ad, the Abbasid chief judge through whom the prisoner appeals.

17.2.1-2.meaning: “The enemies’ wading in”, their meddling and hostile talk.

20.1.2.head: السَّوِيَّة
20.1.2.meaning: Equal treatment, especially of parties to a dispute.

25.2.1.head: فَلَجَ
25.2.1.meaning: Prevailed in an argument or legal case.

26.2.2.head: مَصدَر
26.2.2.meaning: Departure from the watering place, hence our return.

28.2.2.head: أَشادَ
28.2.2.meaning: To proclaim something and make it widely known.
